changes.before: Replace other = values with other = values.dup. What prints?
changes.after: Two names can refer to the same array, a collection of items in order.

before: [1, 2] creates an Array containing two elements. After other = values, both names refer to the same Array object. Assignment does not recursively copy its elements.
other << 3 appends to that shared array. The << method is written like an operator here.

values.dup makes a separate outer Array. It still shares any nested mutable objects, so this simple scalar example is not a deep-copy guarantee.

Here dup takes no explicit argument: its receiver is values. Appending to the new outer array leaves the original outer array unchanged.
```ruby
values = [1]
copy = values.dup
copy << 2
puts values.inspect
puts copy.inspect
```
It prints:
```text
[1]
[1, 2]
```
inspect returns text representing an object; puts writes that text. Here the array representation includes brackets and entries.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby

other = values
other << 3
puts values.inspect
```
Expected output or behavior: [1, 2, 3]. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Here assigning values to other does not make a new array.
The write uses other. The print later uses values.
Put three at the end of the array both names refer to.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
values = [1, 2]
other = values
other << 3
puts values.inspect
```
The output is `[1, 2, 3]`. The change is visible through values because there is just one array.
Use dup to make a separate outer array before appending.
